title: Ready to Fight Tonight: Why NATO's Digital Readiness Cannot Wait Until 2030
summary: Reflections from NATO Edge 26 on the shift from peacetime efficiency to operational readiness, and what it means for the technology supporting modern defence.
body_markdown:
*Reflections from NATO Edge 26 on the shift from peacetime efficiency to operational readiness, and what it means for the technology supporting modern defence.*


At NATO Edge 26 in İzmir, one message stood out: readiness cannot be treated as a future ambition. It must be reflected in the capabilities, infrastructure and partnerships that NATO and its Allies can depend upon today.


During the Leaders’ Fireside: Readiness discussion, senior military leaders and defence industry representatives explored what it takes to translate technological progress into operational capability. While the conversation covered everything from industrial capacity to artificial intelligence, an important distinction emerged between planning for future capability and being prepared to operate under the conditions that exist now.


For NATO, this distinction is increasingly significant. Digital systems underpin the ability to communicate, share intelligence, coordinate across domains and maintain command and control. Their reliability is therefore inseparable from the Alliance’s wider operational readiness.


NATO’s Digital Transformation Implementation Strategy 2.0 establishes a roadmap extending through 2030, with secure, resilient and interoperable capabilities at its centre. But delivering against that longer-term ambition must go hand in hand with strengthening the systems available to military personnel today.


The challenge, then, is not simply to accelerate digital transformation. It is to ensure that these capabilities can support modern operations when infrastructure is disrupted, resources are constrained and the operating environment is contested.


## From peacetime efficiency to operational readiness


One of the most compelling observations came from Air Chief Marshal Sir Johnny Stringer, NATO’s Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe (DSACEUR), who reflected on how three decades of relative peace had shaped approaches to military support and industrial capacity.


During this period, practices built around efficiency, predictable demand and just-in-time delivery became increasingly established. These approaches have clear economic advantages, but they also raise questions about whether systems and supply chains designed for peacetime conditions can respond to the demands of sustained conflict.


For a defensive alliance, the ability to absorb an initial attack and maintain operational effectiveness is fundamental to credible deterrence. That requires sufficient capacity, resilience and support to continue operating when circumstances are far less predictable.


The same principle applies to digital infrastructure. Technology that performs effectively under normal conditions is not necessarily prepared for an environment where connectivity is disrupted, physical infrastructure is threatened or demand exceeds planned capacity. Availability and efficiency remain important, but they cannot be the only measures of success.


This represents an important shift in how digital capability should be understood. Communications networks, operational software and information-sharing systems are not simply supporting services. They form part of the infrastructure through which military operations are coordinated and sustained. Investing in digital readiness must therefore be considered alongside investment in more traditional defence capabilities, rather than treated as a separate technology modernisation exercise.


## Readiness must be built and funded before it is needed


The discussion also highlighted the importance of industrial readiness and the relationship between governments and their technology suppliers. Lt Gen Jari Mikkonen, Deputy Chief of Staff, Armament and Logistics for the Finnish Defence Forces, outlined Finland’s approach to ensuring that critical industrial capabilities remain available during a crisis.


Central to this model is identifying the products, services and technologies that are essential to national defence, establishing the required level of readiness and creating the financial arrangements necessary to maintain it.


Importantly, readiness extends well beyond the availability of equipment. It includes production capacity, supply chains, maintenance, software updates and access to specialist personnel. These considerations are just as relevant to digital capability as they are to traditional military logistics.


A digital system may be technically capable of supporting an operation, but its operational value also depends on the availability of infrastructure, expertise, maintenance and ongoing support. Ensuring that these elements remain available under pressure requires preparation long before they are needed.


There is also a commercial reality to consider. Maintaining additional capacity and specialist resources carries a cost, even when that capacity is not being used. Where governments require a level of readiness beyond normal commercial demand, that expectation needs to be supported by appropriate funding and long-term commitments.


For NATO and its Allies, the implication is clear: industrial and digital readiness cannot depend solely on suppliers being able to respond when a crisis emerges. The capacity to respond must already exist.


## Closing the gap between innovation and operational capability


A further theme was the pace at which emerging technologies can move from development into operational use. Dr Frank Dirksen, Chief Commercial Officer at Helsing, emphasised the value of testing emerging capabilities against real military requirements and allowing demonstrated performance to inform procurement decisions.


This raises a broader challenge for defence organisations. Technology is evolving rapidly, particularly in areas such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and decision support, while acquisition processes often operate on considerably longer timelines. Responsible procurement and operational urgency should not be competing priorities.


As Lt Gen Mikkonen noted, procurement regulations play an essential role in safeguarding public funds, but they can also slow the adoption of new technologies. The challenge is to maintain appropriate oversight while enabling capabilities that have demonstrated operational value to be procured and deployed more quickly.


Field evaluations, adaptable procurement frameworks and closer engagement between industry and military users can all contribute to reducing this gap. They also create opportunities for capabilities to evolve as operational requirements change, rather than becoming fixed to specifications established years earlier.


This is where the distinction between readiness today and transformation by 2030 becomes particularly important. Long-term capability programmes remain necessary. NATO must continue planning for the technologies, architectures and operational requirements of the next decade. But those programmes cannot replace the need to strengthen the capabilities available to military personnel now.


Digital readiness requires progress on both timelines: investing in future capability while ensuring today’s systems can adapt to emerging threats and operational demands.


## Resilience must be demonstrated, not assumed


The discussion also reinforced the importance of designing technology around the conditions in which it will actually be used. Modern military operations increasingly depend on a combination of cloud infrastructure, deployed systems, communications networks and local computing capabilities. Each has a role in providing the scale, flexibility and responsiveness required across different operational environments.


However, the conditions experienced at the tactical edge can differ significantly from those at operational headquarters. These challenges are particularly apparent in[disconnected, degraded, intermittent and low-bandwidth (DDIL) environments](https://mattermost.com/blog/mission-readiness-in-ddil-environments/) , where maintaining operational coordination requires systems designed to function without continuous connectivity.


Resilience therefore depends on understanding those differences and designing capabilities that can continue supporting essential functions when normal operating assumptions no longer apply.


Air Chief Marshal Sir Johnny Stringer also emphasised the importance of using NATO exercises to test not only military procedures, but the underlying infrastructure and industrial capacity required to sustain operations. This is an important consideration. Exercises provide an opportunity to identify weaknesses before they become operational failures, assess whether industry can meet sustained demand and understand where technology or infrastructure limitations may affect operational plans.


For digital capabilities, this means moving beyond demonstrations in controlled environments and validating how systems perform when operating conditions deteriorate. Readiness cannot be established through technical specifications alone. It has to be demonstrated through realistic testing, continuous improvement and close cooperation between defence organisations and their technology partners.


## Digital readiness is a shared responsibility


Taken together, the discussions at NATO Edge point towards a broader understanding of operational readiness. It is not enough for technology to be innovative, scalable or secure under normal conditions. It must also be deployable, supportable and resilient in the environments where it is expected to operate.


This places greater responsibility on industry to understand operational requirements and demonstrate how its capabilities contribute to mission continuity. It also requires governments and defence organisations to create the procurement, funding and testing conditions that make sustained readiness possible.


For organisations such as Mattermost, working in sovereign, mission-critical collaboration, these considerations are particularly relevant. The ability to maintain coordination, share operational information and retain control over critical communications infrastructure is an essential part of digital resilience.


No single technology or supplier can deliver NATO’s digital readiness. It depends on an ecosystem of capabilities that can work together across organisations, national boundaries and operational environments, while respecting the sovereign requirements of individual Allies.


Ultimately, the challenge raised at NATO Edge is not whether NATO recognises the importance of digital transformation. It is whether the Alliance and its industry partners can translate that ambition into dependable capability at the pace required.


The technology of 2030 will undoubtedly play an important role in NATO’s future. But credible deterrence also depends on the systems, infrastructure and partnerships available today.


To be ready to fight tonight, digital readiness must be more than a future objective. It must be an operational reality.
